# One Memory, Many Machines: A field guide to shared CXL memory

> What shared CXL memory is, why hardware coherence covers only a sliver of it, and how to share data on it anyway: a general-audience walk from the memory wall to our lab's Megalon (OSDI '26) and Prism (SOSP '26).

A general-audience explainer by Kiran Hombal and Jiyu Hu of shared CXL memory,
based on the authors' papers Megalon (OSDI 2026, best-paper
nominee) and Prism (SOSP 2026) and a talk they gave at ByteDance.
Every number on the page names its source. Values read off a paper
figure are labeled as such in the figure's caption.

## Read this instead of the HTML

## The one-paragraph version

CXL 3.x lets several hosts map the same terabytes of memory. In the
hardware model both papers target, only a few hundred MB stay coherent
across hosts (the SCR); the terabytes beyond (the LNR) can silently serve
stale caches. Megalon shares data anyway by splitting the metadata:
replicate the big, cold index per host, keep tiny hot coherence records
in the SCR, and order everything through a shared log in CXL, for up to
10x the prior approach under writes and 15x on reads. Prism shows that
disk-born LSMs are the right index for this memory because their
updatable surface area is tiny, adds a Bounded Updatable Layer sized to
the SCR, and beats ported in-memory indexes by up to 9.4x and a
Tigon-style index by up to 15.1x.
